MapMaker lessons: Grade 8 US History

Ten lessons that teach Grade 8 US History with National Geographic MapMaker maps, arranged by topic in the order most courses teach them. Each one pairs a map with an inquiry, a Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and a separate teacher page with the answers.

10 lessons · US History · no account or login needed

Road to revolution and the Revolution

  • 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

    Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

    For teachers: notes and answers

Confederation and the Constitution

  • Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: The early republic

    Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.

    For teachers: notes and answers

  • We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: The early republic

    See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.

    For teachers: notes and answers

The early republic

  • Presidential Elections, 1796 and 1800

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

    Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and find two Supreme Court cases that shaped the new government.

    For teachers: notes and answers

  • The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.

    For teachers: notes and answers

  • The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

    For teachers: notes and answers

Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

  • Roads, Trails, and Rails West

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

    For teachers: notes and answers

Reform and the road to war

  • US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.

    For teachers: notes and answers

The Civil War

  • Civil War Battlefields

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    See how the United States split in 1861, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.

    For teachers: notes and answers

  • The Battle of Vicksburg

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

    Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.

    For teachers: notes and answers

In every lesson

  • A MapMaker map that opens straight from the page, with each layer’s source listed. No account or login is needed.
  • An inquiry with a compelling question and questions you can pick from, each answered from the map.
  • A Word student sheet in English and Spanish that you can edit, print or open in Google Docs.
  • A separate teacher page, and a Word file, with where to find each answer on the map, what to accept, common misunderstandings, key words and standards.
  • Links to how-to videos, a link to Vera, and a prompt for your own AI tool.

Make your own questions with Vera

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.4(C)

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Revolutionary War BattlesWhat it shows: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates, a picture and a short account. The winner is shown only by the diamond's color, as listed in the legend (American Victory or British Victory); the pop-up does not state it in words.Source: American Battlefield Trust
Revolutionary War BattlefieldsWhat it shows: Battlefield boundaries (gray) and the core areas where the fighting was heaviest (diagonal stripes). No pop-ups.Source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Turning PointsWhat it shows: Five white circles numbered 1 to 5, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, that appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the event's name, year, a short account (the Battle_details field) and the victor.Source: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources
Thirteen British ColoniesWhat it shows: Colony areas and borders in 1763. The pop-up gives the colony's name.Source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
1763 Proclamation LineWhat it shows: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlementSource: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Ports that supplied armies and moved troops, from New England to the Caribbean and Britain. The legend separates a Major Port City (larger symbol) from a smaller Port. The layer has no pop-ups and no labels.Source: Jay Feyerabend, master's thesis (opens in a new tab), James Madison University (2021)

Bookmarks: Massachusetts.

Inquiry

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one is answered from the map, lists the MapMaker tools it uses, and links to how-to videos. Answers and what to accept are in the teacher notes, linked at the foot of this page.

  1. Where did the war begin?

    Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

    Zoom out until all 21 diamonds show, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Why New York?

    Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group). Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, name the major ports between Boston and Charleston (the layer has no pop-ups, so the battle diamonds and the coastline help), measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. How did 1776 end?

    Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Open the map in MapMaker: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Before you start

British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.

Reading the map

Diamonds mark battles. A battle's pop-up gives its name, dates and story, but not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner, so use the legend. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened. The Key Port Cities layer has no pop-ups: the legend tells a major port from a smaller one.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the war begin? Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord. When was it fought? Use the legend to find out who won. Then click the Boston diamond: how long did the siege of Boston last? Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: miles
  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one and write its name under the year it was fought. Use the legend to mark who won. Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
  3. Why New York? In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (it's inside Revolutionary War Battlefields). Use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port. Boston and Charleston are major ports: which other major ports lie between them? The layer has no pop-ups, so use the coastline and the battle diamonds nearby to name them. Measure from New York to Philadelphia and from New York to Boston. Looking at the map, what could a navy based at New York reach? New York to Philadelphia: miles. New York to Boston: miles
  4. How did 1776 end? Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear, then follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. When was each fought, and who won? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: miles

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about 1775–1776 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicWestward expansion and Manifest Destiny (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Trails WestWhat it shows: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each a dotted line in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up is titled with the trail's name and gives a short history with places, dates and distances.Source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information
Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Five transcontinental lines as thick colored lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific), Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) and Southern Pacific. No pop-up. In the Railroads group.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Railroads 1826 to 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: All railroad lines built from 1826 to 1911, as thin gray lines. Each pop-up gives the railroad's name (where recorded) and the year it was in operation by. In the Railroads group.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Indigenous Territories (off when the map opens)What it shows: Approximate territories of Indigenous nations, from a community-made map, each shaded in its own color with the nation's name appearing when zoomed in. Not listed in the legend. No pop-up.Source: Native Land Digital

Bookmarks: none.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one is answered from the map, lists the MapMaker tools it uses, and links to how-to videos. Answers and what to accept are in the teacher notes, linked at the foot of this page.

  1. Where did the trails begin?

    Click three trails (use the legend to tell them apart) and note from each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. How far, and how many?

    Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, just east of Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Whose land?

    Turn on Indigenous Territories in Map layers and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from end to end. Was the West empty land when the trails were built? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. From trails to rails

    Turn on the Railroads group in Map layers. Using the legend, which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line to see when it was in operation (the thick transcontinental lines have no pop-up).

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Open the map in MapMaker: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Before you start

In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.

Reading the map

Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them, and clicking a trail opens its pop-up. City and state names are part of the basemap. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, named in the legend, and thin gray lines are other railroads; only the thin gray lines have pop-ups. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color, and its name appears when you zoom in. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the trails begin? Click three of the dotted trail lines (the legend shows which color is which trail). From each pop-up, where did the trail start and end? In which state do most of the trails start?
  2. How far, and how many? Click the Oregon Trail (find its color in the legend). How long was it, and how many people traveled it? Then use Measure for a straight line from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, next to Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon. Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: miles
  3. Whose land? In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories. Zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from one end to the other. Name two nations whose land it crossed. Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
  4. From trails to rails In Map layers, turn on Railroads. Use the legend to find the Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines. Which trails do they follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line: when was it in operation by?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the journey west that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Before you start

George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.

The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name and its number of electors. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); use the legend. Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases; each pop-up has a Why here part. Using both maps, describe where each party was strong and where the two parties competed. Changed completely: , with electors.

Before you start

In 1803 the United States bought France's claim to a huge area west of the Mississippi River. Native nations lived on and governed most of that land; the National Park Service says the expedition met more than 50 Tribal Nations. President Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to explore it and look for a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The expedition set out in 1803 and returned in 1806.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click an area to see its name. Use the legend: green is the land Britain gave up to the United States in 1783; yellow is the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Edges of the purchase settled later have other colors or stripes. A purple line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, and small symbols mark the Corps' approximate campsites; the line and the symbols have no pop-ups. United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens and show today's landscape. Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. A bigger country Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark and use the legend. Compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of the United States in 1783. About how much bigger did the country become? Click the Louisiana Purchase: how much land was it, and what did it cost? Size: about million acres. Price: $ million.
  2. Why New Orleans? In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio River and the Missouri River. Which river regions are they? Zoom out and follow the rivers on the map: into which big river do they flow, and which city sits near its mouth? In 1800 farmers west of the Appalachians sent their crops to market by river. Why did control of New Orleans matter to them?
  3. Up the Missouri Open the Up the Missouri bookmark and follow the trail line and the campsite symbols up the Missouri River. In Map layers, turn off United States Watersheds and turn on Biomes, then click the shading along the route. Which biome covers the Great Plains (the first line of the pop-up)? Look at where the campsites sit: why do you think the Corps traveled along rivers?
  4. Across the Rockies Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Where does the trail line leave the yellow Louisiana Purchase? Was the Pacific coast part of it? Zoom out and use Measure to find the straight-line distance from the trail's eastern end, at Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (where the Ohio River begins), to its western end on the Pacific coast. Straight-line distance: miles. The trail itself is about 4,900 miles long.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers. Remember that the map has no layer for the Native nations who already lived on this land; use what Before you start says about them. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the Louisiana Purchase that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Teacher notes: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.4(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.6

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map and check it loads. Every layer is on except Key Port Cities, which students turn on for question 3. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet separately). No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved, so students who sketch should finish in one session or take a screenshot. Read the answers on the teacher page.

Answer notes

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

1. Where did the war begin?

Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

Where to find it on the mapMassachusetts bookmark. Lexington and Concord pop-up, the date line under the title: April 19, 1775. Legend (Revolutionary War Battles): blue diamond = American Victory, red = British Victory. Boston pop-up: April 19, 1775 to March 17, 1776, about 11 months. Measure tool, Boston to Concord: about 16 miles (accept 15 to 17).

NotesUse the Revolutionary War Battles legend for the result.

2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

Zoom out until all 21 diamonds show, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

Where to find it on the mapRevolutionary War Battles layer, zoomed out to the whole east coast: 21 diamonds. Each pop-up's date line gives the year; the diamond color and the legend give the winner. The colony comes from the Thirteen British Colonies layer or the pop-up's account.

Accept answers thatA good answer lists most of the 21 battles under the right year (8 in 1775, 13 in 1776), names Massachusetts, New York, Virginia and Quebec for 1775 and adds North Carolina, South Carolina, New Jersey and Rhode Island for 1776, and says that the fighting began around Boston and then spread along the coast, with most battles from August 1776 in New York and New Jersey, where the British won nearly all of them.

Answer key
YearAmerican victoriesBritish victories
1775 (8 battles)American victories: Lexington and Concord, Boston (siege) and Gloucester (Massachusetts); Fort Ticonderoga and Crown Point (New York); Great Bridge (Virginia)British victories: Bunker Hill (Massachusetts); Quebec (Quebec)
1776 (13 battles)American victories: Moores Creek Bridge (North Carolina); Sullivan's Island and Breach Inlet (South Carolina); Gwynn's Island (Virginia); Trenton (New Jersey)British victories: Brooklyn, Valcour Island, Pell's Point, White Plains, Fort Washington (New York); Fort Lee, Mount Holly (New Jersey); Newport (Rhode Island)

3. Why New York?

Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group). Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, name the major ports between Boston and Charleston (the layer has no pop-ups, so the battle diamonds and the coastline help), measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

Where to find it on the mapKey Port Cities layer, legend: larger symbol = Major Port City, smaller = Port. Five major ports: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Norfolk and Charleston, so the three between Boston and Charleston are New York, Philadelphia and Norfolk. The layer has no pop-ups or labels: New York sits by the Brooklyn diamond, Norfolk by the Great Bridge diamond, and Philadelphia is up the Delaware River south-west of Trenton. Measure tool: New York to Philadelphia about 80 miles (accept 75 to 85); New York to Boston about 190 miles (accept 180 to 200).

Accept answers thatA good answer names at least New York and Philadelphia, gives both distances within range, and says that New York is in the middle of the coast, a day or two's sail from Boston, Philadelphia and the Chesapeake, with a deep harbor and the Hudson River leading north, so a navy there could reach the other big ports and cut New England off from the rest of the colonies.

NotesAccept Norfolk if a student works it out; it is the hardest to name without labels. Background for teachers: Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust (opens in a new tab).

4. How did 1776 end?

Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

Where to find it on the mapTurning Points circles 4 (Fall of New York City, 1776, Victor: Britain) and 5 (Washington Strikes Back, 1776, Victor: United States); the pop-up's Battle details text tells the story of each. Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups: Fort Washington, November 16, 1776, and Fort Lee, November 20, 1776, red = British Victory; Trenton, December 26, 1776, blue = American Victory. Measure tool, New York City to Trenton: about 52 miles (accept 48 to 56).

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The early war was fought in Massachusetts.” By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.
  • “The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.” Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.
  • “The Americans lost every battle in 1776.” The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

Key words

  • siege
  • militia
  • Continental Army
  • Loyalist
  • harbor
  • campaign
  • retreat

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
TX 8.4(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Explain the issues surrounding important events of the American Revolution, including declaring independence; fighting the battles of Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, and Yorktown; enduring the winter at Valley Forge; and signing the Treaty of Paris of 1783
FL SS.8.A.3.6Framework: FloridaStandard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of the American Revolution

Lessons › Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Teacher notes: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicWestward expansion and Manifest Destiny (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.11(A)
    • TX 8.6(B)
    • TX 8.6(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.4.1

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map in MapMaker. The Railroads group and Indigenous Territories are off at the start; students turn them on in Map layers for questions 3 and 4. There are no bookmarks, so students zoom and pan. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet). Read the answers on the teacher page. No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved.

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

1. Where did the trails begin?

Click three trails (use the legend to tell them apart) and note from each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

Where to find it on the mapTrails West pop-ups (title is the trail name, the text gives the places). Most trails start in Missouri: Independence (Oregon, California), St. Joseph (Pony Express), St. Louis (Butterfield Overland) or Missouri in general (Santa Fe). On the map, the Mormon Pioneer trail's eastern end is at Nauvoo, Illinois, on the Mississippi, and its pop-up mentions Nauvoo and Omaha.

Accept answers thatMissouri. For why, a good answer uses the map: Missouri was at the western edge of the settled states and on the Missouri River, so it was the last place to buy supplies and the river was the way in.

Answer key
TrailFromTo
OregonFrom: Independence, MissouriTo: Willamette River valley, near Portland, Oregon
CaliforniaFrom: Independence, Missouri, and Omaha, NebraskaTo: Northern California
Mormon PioneerFrom: Nauvoo, Illinois (the line's eastern end on the map), then past Omaha, NebraskaTo: Salt Lake City, Utah
Santa FeFrom: MissouriTo: Santa Fe, New Mexico
Pony ExpressFrom: St. Joseph, MissouriTo: Sacramento, California
Butterfield OverlandFrom: St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee, via Fort Smith, ArkansasTo: San Francisco, California
Old SpanishFrom: Abiquiú, New MexicoTo: Los Angeles, California

2. How far, and how many?

Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, just east of Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

Where to find it on the mapOregon Trail pop-up: about 2,000 miles (3,219 km); 300,000 to 400,000 people between 1840 and 1860. Measure tool, Independence to Portland: about 1,500 miles (accept 1,450 to 1,550).

Accept answers thatThe trail is about 500 miles longer than the straight line. A good answer says the dotted line bends to follow rivers (the pop-up names the Platte, North Platte, Snake and Columbia) for water and grass, and crosses the mountains through passes rather than straight over them.

3. Whose land?

Turn on Indigenous Territories in Map layers and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from end to end. Was the West empty land when the trails were built? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

Where to find it on the mapIndigenous Territories layer (off at start; names draw when zoomed in). Any trail runs through a continuous patchwork of shaded territories from Missouri to the coast; for example the Oregon Trail crosses lands labeled for the Kaw, Pawnee, Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Shoshone, Nez Perce and others. Accept any two names read from the map.

Accept answers thatNo, the land was not empty: the layer shows nations' territories along the whole trail. For the second part, a good answer reasons from the map that hundreds of thousands of travelers, their wagons and animals crossed these lands, so it could mean lost hunting grounds and grass, disease, pressure on water, forts and settlements along the route, and later loss of the land itself; any reasoned effect, positive or negative, that connects the trail to the people living there is acceptable.

4. From trails to rails

Turn on the Railroads group in Map layers. Using the legend, which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line to see when it was in operation (the thick transcontinental lines have no pop-up).

Where to find it on the mapLegend: Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) are thick colored lines running from Omaha across Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada to Sacramento. Compare with the dotted California and Mormon Pioneer trails (and the Pony Express across Nevada). Railroads 1826 to 1911 pop-up: "Railroad in operation by:" followed by a year; any year the student reads is fine. The California Trail pop-up says the trail was used until 1869, when the transcontinental railroad was completed.

Accept answers thatThe California and Mormon Pioneer trails (also the Pony Express across Nevada). A good answer notes the railroad runs along the same river valleys and passes the wagon trails used, and gives a year read from a gray line's pop-up.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, one journey sketched on the map with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The West was empty before settlers arrived.” The Indigenous Territories layer shows nations' lands across the whole region the trails crossed.
  • “Everyone went west on the Oregon Trail.” The map shows seven trails, to Oregon, California, Utah, New Mexico and Southern California.
  • “The Pony Express lasted for decades.” Its pop-up says it ran for 18 months, from April 1860 to October 1861.

Key words

  • Manifest Destiny
  • emigrant
  • trail
  • transcontinental railroad
  • telegraph
  • Indigenous nation

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.11(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze how physical characteristics of the environment influenced population distribution, settlement patterns, and economic activities in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.6(B)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Explain the political, economic, and social roots of Manifest Destiny
TX 8.6(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the relationship between the concept of Manifest Destiny and the westward growth of the nation
FL SS.8.A.4.1Framework: FloridaStandard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness

Lessons › US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

Teacher notes: US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicReform and the road to war (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.2

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map in MapMaker. Only US 1850 Original Map is off at the start (the scanned source map, useful for comparing with the traced layers); students turn Underground Railroad Approximate Routes off for question 3. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet). Read the answers on the teacher page. No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved.

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?

1. Free states and slave states

Open the legend for US States and Territories 1850 and count the states in the Free states group and the Slave states group (click a state to read its name in the pop-up). Then click two states to read when each became free or slave. Where is the dividing line in the East?

Where to find it on the mapLegend for US States and Territories 1850: four groups. Following the legend shades, the Free states group has 14 states; Iowa and California sit in the paler Free states and territories by compromise group. The Slave states group has 15 as drawn, counting West Virginia; Texas sits in the paler Slave states and territories by compromise group, and Missouri is drawn twice (once in each slave group), so accept 14 to 16 free and 14 to 16 slave with reasons. Pop-up title gives the state name; the first line gives the year (for example Pennsylvania 1780, Virginia 1788). In the East the shades change along the southern border of Pennsylvania and then the Ohio River.

Answer key
Legend groupStates as drawn
Free states (14)States as drawn: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin
Free states and territories by compromiseStates as drawn: Iowa and California, plus Oregon, Minnesota and the unorganized territories
Slave states (15 as drawn)States as drawn: Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia (part of Virginia in 1850), North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, Missouri
Slave states and territories by compromiseStates as drawn: Texas and Missouri (drawn a second time), plus New Mexico and Utah territories and the Indian Territory (drawn as Oklahoma)

NotesHistorically there were 15 free and 15 slave states in 1850 (Iowa and California free, Texas slave). The legend groups split them by how they became free or slave, so the counts students get depend on which groups they add together; the reasoning matters more than the number.

2. The Missouri Compromise

Find the Missouri Compromise Line (gray dashed) and click it for its pop-up. Which slave state lies mostly north of it, and why does that matter?

Where to find it on the mapMissouri Compromise Line pop-up: title Missouri Compromise Line (36°30′ North), year Enacted 1820, and a note that the line divided future slave and free states west of the Mississippi and that Missouri was the exception because most of it lies north of the parallel. On the map, Missouri (green, slave state shades) sits almost entirely north of the line.

Accept answers that1820; Missouri. A good answer says Missouri was allowed in as a slave state even though it lies north of the line, so the line was a deal, not a rule that applied everywhere, and it set up the argument over every new state and territory. Mentioning Maine as the free state admitted at the same time is extra.

3. The internal slave trade

Follow the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade (turn Underground Railroad Approximate Routes off in Map layers to see them clearly). Click the states where the lines begin and where they come together to read their names. Where do the lines reach the coast? The lines have no arrows, so students infer the direction from the pattern and what they have learned.

Where to find it on the mapInternal Routes of the US Slave Trade, solid black lines (no pop-up). Reading them against the state pop-ups: several lines start in Virginia (one from near the Ohio border and one from Kentucky join them), one starts in North Carolina, and they run south and west to meet in central Alabama and at the Mississippi coast in Louisiana. They reach the coast at New Orleans and the Gulf (Louisiana, Alabama) and on the Atlantic off South Carolina.

Accept answers thatA good answer names Virginia (and Kentucky or North Carolina) at one end and Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, with New Orleans on the Gulf, at the other, and says the lines join up as they head south and west toward the ports. From that pattern and from class, students should say enslaved people were moved from the older Upper South to the Deep South and the Gulf, where cotton and sugar plantations wanted labor; accept any direction argued from the map plus a reason.

4. Routes to freedom

Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark and follow the orange Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River; the Cities labels appear when zoomed in. Where do they lead, and why do many continue to Canada?

Where to find it on the mapIllinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes (orange lines) and Cities (orange dots in the US, black dots in Canada; labels draw when zoomed in). Routes run north across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Lake Erie and the Detroit River, at Cleveland, Ashtabula, Toledo and Detroit, and on to the black dots at Chatham and Toronto (Ontario) and Montreal (Quebec).

Accept answers thatNorth to the Great Lakes and across into Canada. A good answer gives two or three town names from the map and explains that freedom seekers were not safe in free states (after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 they could be captured and returned), so Canada, outside the United States, was the safer end of the route.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch that marks free and slave states and one route (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Common misunderstandings

  • “Freedom seekers were safe once they reached a free state.” After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 they could be captured in free states, which is why many routes on the map continue to Canada.
  • “The Underground Railroad was a real railroad.” The routes on the map are paths people walked, rode or sailed, with help along the way; the name borrowed railroad words.
  • “Every Northern state banned slavery at the same time.” The pop-ups give a different year for each free state.

Key words

  • free state
  • slave state
  • Missouri Compromise
  • Fugitive Slave Act
  • Underground Railroad
  • freedom seeker
  • abolition

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
FL SS.8.A.5.2Framework: FloridaStandard: Analyze the role of slavery in the development of sectional conflict

Lessons › Civil War Battlefields

Teacher notes: Civil War Battlefields

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicThe Civil War (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.4

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map in MapMaker: every layer is on at the start and there are no bookmarks, so students zoom to Virginia, Washington, D.C., Maryland and Pennsylvania themselves. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet). Read the answers on the teacher page. No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved.

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War?

1. A nation divided

Open the legend and match each state's shade in U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to its group: which seceded before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union? State names are labeled on the map.

Where to find it on the mapLegend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863): the groups are Union Free State, Union slave state (border state), Slave state seceding before Fort Sumter, April 1861, Slave state seceding after Fort Sumter, April 1861, and Territories. State names are labels on the layer; zoom in if a label is hidden. Counts from the layer: 7 before, 4 after, 5 border states.

Answer key
GroupStates on the map
Seceded before Fort Sumter (7)States on the map: South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Texas
Seceded after Fort Sumter (4)States on the map: Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee
Union slave states, the border states (5)States on the map: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, West Virginia
Union free states (19)States on the map: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Kansas, California, Oregon

NotesWest Virginia split from Virginia and joined the Union as a state in June 1863, which is why it appears on this 1863 map. The two Union shades are close (dark blue and lighter blue), so students may need the legend side by side with the map.

2. The border states

Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? Using the legend shades of those two states, what would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?

Where to find it on the mapZoom to the District of Columbia (a small unshaded area labeled on the States layer). Its neighbors are Maryland (legend: Union slave state, border state) and Virginia (legend: Slave state seceding after Fort Sumter). The white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy runs right past the capital.

Accept answers thatMaryland and Virginia. A good answer uses the legend to say Virginia had seceded, so if Maryland had left too, Washington would have been surrounded by Confederate states and cut off from the rest of the Union.

3. Railroads, North and South

Compare the Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy (a white dashed line). Turning the States layer off in Map layers makes the lines easier to see. Which side had more railroads, and why would that matter in a war?

Where to find it on the mapRailroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer and the Boundary between Union and Confederacy line (legend: white dashed). The lines are visibly denser north of the boundary, above all between the Mississippi River and the Atlantic coast. The map shows lines, not mileage.

Accept answers thatThe North (Union side). A good answer says a denser network let the Union move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther, keep armies supplied, and shift troops between fronts; the South had fewer lines and gaps between them.

4. Where were the battles?

Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, and click the tan battlefield areas for names, sizes and state. Where were most battles fought, and which were fought in Union states (check the state's shade in the legend)?

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefield Boundary pop-ups: the title is the battle name; Battlefield Acres and State Name (two-letter code) are listed below. Most tan areas are in Virginia (the layer has far more in VA than in any other state). Union states by the legend: Maryland (border state) has Antietam (34,937 acres), South Mountain, Monocacy, Boonsboro, Williamsport, Hancock and Folck's Mill; Pennsylvania (Union free state) has Gettysburg (73,551 acres) and Hanover. If a pop-up says 1 of 2, a core area sits under the boundary; use the arrows.

Accept answers thatMost battles were in the Confederate states, above all Virginia, between the two capitals. Any battle named from a Maryland or Pennsylvania pop-up, most often Antietam or Gettysburg.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch of the front line with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Common misunderstandings

  • “All slave states joined the Confederacy.” The legend shows five slave states that stayed in the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia.
  • “The war was fought evenly across the North and the South.” Most battlefields on the map are in Confederate states, above all Virginia.

  • Union
  • Confederacy
  • border state
  • Fort Sumter
  • battlefield
  • railroad network

Teacher notes: The Battle of Vicksburg

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicThe Civil War
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(C)

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map in MapMaker and open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Civil War Battlefields is off at the start; students turn it on for questions 3 and 4. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet). Read the answers on the teacher page. No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved.

Answer notes

Compelling question

Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?

1. Why Vicksburg?

Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Vicksburg is the yellow pin. Look at where it sits on the Mississippi River. Zoom in until the railroads draw and follow the line east from Vicksburg to Jackson, Mississippi, the state capital, which is a basemap label (not a pin). Why would both sides want the city?

Where to find it on the mapThe Battle of Vicksburg bookmark; yellow pin at Vicksburg on a bend of the Mississippi; Railroads 1826 to 1911 layer, which draws when zoomed in to about 1:1,500,000 or closer; Jackson is a label on the Modern Antique basemap about 40 miles east.

Accept answers thatA good answer says Vicksburg sits on the river, so whoever held it controlled traffic on the Mississippi, and that its railroad linked the river to Jackson and the rest of the Confederacy, so it was both a river stronghold and a rail junction. Mentioning the bluffs or guns is extra, not on the map.

2. Grant's route

Find the dark pins and put them in order along Grant's route: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend, then Edwards. Which side of the river is each on? Measure the straight-line distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.

Where to find it on the mapKey Places in the Union March to Vicksburg pins, read against the river and the basemap state labels: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times are on the west (Louisiana) bank; Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards are on the east (Mississippi) side. Measure tool, Milliken's Bend pin to Bruinsburg Bend pin: about 33 miles in a straight line (accept 31 to 36).

Accept answers thatA good answer notices that Vicksburg's pin sits on the river between Milliken's Bend (north) and Bruinsburg Bend (south), so Grant could not cross right at the city; he marched down the far bank, out of reach of the city, crossed well to the south, then turned back toward Vicksburg from the east (Edwards).

3. The battles of May 1863

Turn on Civil War Battlefields in Map layers and click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg, and east toward Jackson. Put the battles in order by date from the pop-ups.

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefields pop-ups: the name is in bold and the dates below it. Port Gibson's pop-up says 1 of 2; both entries are the same battle. Grand Gulf (April 29, 1863), on the river just north of Bruinsburg, is the Union navy's failed attack before the crossing; accept it if students include it.

Answer key
BattleDates
Port GibsonDates: May 1, 1863
RaymondDates: May 12, 1863
Jackson, MississippiDates: May 14, 1863
Champion HillDates: May 16, 1863
Big Black River BridgeDates: May 17, 1863
VicksburgDates: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863

4. Splitting the Confederacy

Zoom out to see the whole Mississippi River from Memphis to the Gulf. With Civil War Battlefields on, click the diamond at Port Hudson, Louisiana, south of Vicksburg, for its dates. Using the state names on the basemap, which states lie west of the river, and what did the Union control once both Vicksburg and Port Hudson had surrendered?

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefields pop-up for Port Hudson: May 21, 1863 – July 9, 1863. Vicksburg pop-up: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863. Basemap state labels west of the river: Louisiana (most of it), Arkansas, Texas (and Missouri further north, Union side).

Accept answers thatPort Hudson surrendered on July 9, 1863, five days after Vicksburg. A good answer names Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas west of the river and says the Union then controlled the whole Mississippi, so those Confederate states were cut off from the rest of the Confederacy and the river was open to Union ships and closed to Confederate supplies.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, Grant's route sketched on the map (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Common misunderstandings

  • “Grant attacked Vicksburg straight across the river.” The key places show he marched south on the Louisiana side and crossed at Bruinsburg, well south of the city.
  • “Vicksburg fell in a single battle.” Its pop-up gives May 18 to July 4, 1863: a siege of about six weeks.
  • “Gettysburg was the only turning point of July 1863.” Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, the day after Gettysburg ended, and gave the Union the Mississippi.

Key words

  • siege
  • campaign
  • bluff
  • gunboat
  • supply line
  • surrender

TX 8.10(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
FL SS.8.A.5.1Framework: FloridaStandard: Explain the causes, course, and consequence of the Civil War (sectionalism, slavery, states' rights, balance of power in the Senate)

Teacher notes: We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicConfederation and the Constitution (also fits: The early republic)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Civ.5.6-8
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • TX 8.17(A)
    • TX 8.4(D)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.10
    • FL SS.8.A.3.11

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map and check it loads. House seats in 1793, House seats today and Ratifying the Constitution are off at the start; the basemap has no place names, so students click for a state's name. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet separately). No account or login is needed; sketches are not saved. Read the answers on the teacher page.

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the Constitution balance large and small states, and how close did it come to being rejected?

1. Who lived where in 1790?

Open The states in 1790 bookmark. Students compare the pie sizes to find the most populous state, then click the pies and read the 1790 census line of each pop-up to find the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.

Where to find it on the mapThe states in 1790 bookmark; Population in 1790 layer. Biggest pie and pop-up first line: Virginia, 747,610 people (Kentucky is counted separately; Massachusetts, which then included Maine, is next with 475,327). The percentage in the first line of each pop-up ("1790 census: … people, … of them enslaved (…%)") is above 25 in five states, listed below. Legend: blue = free people, orange-red = enslaved people.

Answer key
StatePeopleEnslavedShare enslaved
South CarolinaPeople: 249,073Enslaved: 107,094Share enslaved: 43.0%
VirginiaPeople: 747,610Enslaved: 292,627Share enslaved: 39.1%
GeorgiaPeople: 82,548Enslaved: 29,264Share enslaved: 35.5%
MarylandPeople: 319,728Enslaved: 103,036Share enslaved: 32.2%
North CarolinaPeople: 393,751Enslaved: 100,572Share enslaved: 25.5%

2. Seats in Congress

Turn on House seats in 1793. Students use the labels (abbreviation and seats) and the legend to find the states with the most and fewest seats, then read the pop-up to compare House seats with senators.

Where to find it on the mapHouse seats in 1793 layer. Labels and legend (darkest class, 13 to 19 seats): Virginia, VA: 19, the most of the 105 seats. Palest class (1 to 2 seats): Delaware, DE: 1, the fewest; Vermont, Rhode Island, Kentucky and Georgia have 2. Pop-up, third line: "plus 2 senators, like every state".

Accept answers thatA good answer names Virginia (19) and Delaware (1), says every state had two senators, and explains the Great Compromise in its own words: House seats follow population, which suited the large states, while the equal Senate protected the small ones. The pop-up also gives the ratio, one seat for every 33,000 people counted.

3. The three-fifths clause

Students click Virginia and South Carolina and read the last two lines of each pop-up, which give the seats each would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all, and compare them with the actual seats. Then they look for other states where the two numbers differ.

Where to find it on the mapPopulation in 1790 or House seats in 1793 pop-up, the lines "That gave … House seats in 1793", "If enslaved people had been counted in full" and "If they had not been counted at all". Virginia: 19, 22, 13. South Carolina: 6, 7, 4. Seven states show a higher seat count under the clause than with no count, listed below.

Accept answers thatA good answer gives Virginia 19 and 13 (fill-in) and South Carolina 6 and 4, names at least Virginia, North Carolina, Maryland and South Carolina as states that gained seats, and says that enslaved people were counted for seats but could not vote, so the gain went to the slaveholding states. The seven states gained 15 seats in all (105 instead of 90), Virginia alone 6.

Answer key

VirginiaSeats (three-fifths): 19If counted in full: 22If not counted: 13
North CarolinaSeats (three-fifths): 10If counted in full: 11If not counted: 8
MarylandSeats (three-fifths): 8If counted in full: 9If not counted: 6
South CarolinaSeats (three-fifths): 6If counted in full: 7If not counted: 4
New YorkSeats (three-fifths): 10If counted in full: 10If not counted: 9
GeorgiaSeats (three-fifths): 2If counted in full: 2If not counted: 1
KentuckySeats (three-fifths): 2If counted in full: 2If not counted: 1

4. How close was ratification?

Turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793 and turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Students click the pies, read the vote line of each pop-up ("Ratified on …: … for, … against") to find the three closest votes, and open both North Carolina pies to explain why there are two.

Where to find it on the mapRatifying the Constitution layer; legend: blue = voted to ratify, orange-red = voted against. Pop-up first line: Rhode Island 34 for, 32 against (label RI 13, May 29, 1790); New York 30–27 (NY 11, July 26, 1788); Massachusetts 187–168 (MA 6, February 6, 1788). By number of votes the next closest are Virginia 89–79 (VA 10) and New Hampshire 57–47 (NH 9, the ninth state, enough to put the Constitution into effect). North Carolina: the NC (1788) pie at Hillsborough, titled "Did not ratify (first convention)", 83 for, 184 against, with a note that a second convention ratified in November 1789; the NC 12 pie at Fayetteville, 194–77, November 21, 1789.

Accept answers thatA good answer names Rhode Island, New York and Massachusetts (accept Virginia or New Hampshire if the student counts the gap in votes rather than the share), and explains that North Carolina's first convention did not ratify and a second one did more than a year later, after Congress had proposed the Bill of Rights. Sources differ on the exact 1788 vote and date; accept the pop-up's figures.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry and George Mason, each with a quote and the principle it argues about (sketches are not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot); or a short talk using the map.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The three-fifths clause gave enslaved people a share of representation.” It gave slaveholding states more seats, not enslaved people a voice: they could not vote. Virginia's pop-up shows 19 seats under the clause, against 13 if enslaved people had not been counted.
  • “Every state ratified the Constitution easily.” Rhode Island ratified by 34 to 32 and New York by 30 to 27, and North Carolina's first convention did not ratify.
  • “Large states had more senators.” Every state had two senators; only House seats followed population.

Key words

  • ratify
  • convention
  • census
  • apportionment
  • Great Compromise
  • three-fifths clause
  • Federalist
  • Anti-Federalist

C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
TX 8.17(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the arguments of the Federalists and Anti-Federalists, including those of Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry, James Madison, and George Mason, and explain how their debates exemplify civil discourse
TX 8.4(D)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the issues of the Constitutional Convention of 1787, including the Great Compromise and the Three-Fifths Compromise
FL SS.8.A.3.10Framework: FloridaStandard: Examine the course and consequences of the Constitutional Convention (New Jersey Plan, Virginia Plan, Great Compromise, Three-Fifths Compromise, compromises regarding taxation and slave trade, Electoral College, state vs. federal power, empowering a president).
FL SS.8.A.3.11Framework: FloridaStandard: Analyze support and opposition (Federalists, Federalist Papers, Anti-Federalists, Bill of Rights) to ratification of the U.S. Constitution.

Teacher notes: Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicConfederation and the Constitution (also fits: The early republic)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Civ.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.Civ.8.6-8
    • C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8
    • TX 8.19(B)
    • TX 8.19(C)
    • FL SS.8.CG.2.5

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Before class

Open the map and zoom to your town to check the basemap labels its public buildings. National Register of Historic Places is off at the start. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet separately). No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved, so students finish in one session or take a screenshot. Read the answers on the teacher page.

Answer notes

Compelling question

Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?

1. Who represents us?

Students zoom to their town on the Topographic basemap and click inside their congressional district to read the pop-up, which names the representative, their party and the district number. Then they zoom out to the whole state and count the blue-outlined districts.

Where to find it on the mapCongressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up: "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]". The district count is the number of blue-outlined areas in the state when zoomed out, which equals the state's House seats after the 2020 census: for example California 52, Texas 38, Florida 28; six states (Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming) have one, shown as the whole state.

Accept answers thatAccept the name and party as the pop-up gives them for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); a seat that has changed hands since the layer was updated may differ. In California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah the district on the November 2026 ballot may differ from the one shown (see the map's description).

2. Rights in public places

Students zoom in on their town until the Topographic basemap labels buildings, pick four public places it shows or that they know (courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place, newspaper office), sketch a pin on each and label it with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Sketches are not saved, so students finish in one session or take a screenshot.

Where to find it on the mapThe Topographic basemap labels schools, churches, courthouses, libraries and city halls in most towns at close zoom. Sketch tool: a pin and a text label at each place. There is no stored answer; the teacher checks the student's screen or screenshot.

Accept answers thatFour pins on public places (not homes), each paired with a right that fits: a newspaper office with freedom of the press, a place of worship with free exercise of religion, city hall or a public square with assembly and petition, a library with speech and the press, a courthouse with due process or a jury trial (Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Amendments). A polling place connects with voting, which later amendments protect (15th, 19th and 26th), so accept it with that note.

3. Responsibilities

Students start from the courthouse or city hall they pinned in question 2, add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens (voting, jury service, paying taxes), and sort the responsibilities into required by law and voluntary.

Where to find it on the mapSketch pins on the student's map, usually at the courthouse (jury service), a polling place such as a school, library or church (voting), and a post office or tax office (paying taxes). There is no stored answer; check the screen or screenshot.

Accept answers thatAt least two pins with a responsibility each, and a sort that puts obeying laws, paying taxes, jury service when called and, for most men aged 18 through 25, Selective Service registration under required by law, and voting, staying informed, volunteering and attending community meetings under voluntary. Accept the point that voting is both a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it.

4. History where we live

Turn on National Register of Historic Places, zoom in until the diamonds appear, and click the two nearest the school. The pop-up gives the address but not the name, so students match the diamond to the basemap label or follow the pop-up's National Archive Information link. Look for a public building and the right or responsibility it connects with.

Where to find it on the mapNational Register of Historic Places layer, on at close zoom. Pop-up: address, city, county, state, resource type and a National Archive Information link; the place name is not shown, so students read it from the basemap label or the National Archives record. Legend: diamond colors for building, structure, district, site and object. If nothing is listed nearby, zoom out to the nearest town.

Accept answers thatTwo places identified by address or name, with a sensible link for any public building: a courthouse with jury service and a fair trial; a post office or newspaper building with sharing news and ideas; a school or library with staying informed. Accept "neither is a public building" with a reason.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from their own map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a screenshot of the sketched map with a short caption, or a short talk using the map. Sketches are not saved between sessions.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The Bill of Rights lists all of a citizen's rights.” The Ninth Amendment says other rights are kept by the people, and later amendments added rights, such as the voting rights in the 15th, 19th and 26th.
  • “Voting is required by law.” No federal law requires it. Serving on a jury when called and paying taxes are required.
  • “Everyone in a state votes for the same representative.” Each district elects its own representative; senators are chosen by the whole state.

Key words

  • amendment
  • Bill of Rights
  • civil liberties
  • citizen
  • responsibility
  • congressional district
  • representative
  • jury

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Civ.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain specific roles played by citizens (such as voters, jurors, taxpayers, members of the armed forces, petitioners, protesters, and office-holders).
C3 D2.Civ.8.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Analyze ideas and principles contained in the founding documents of the United States, and explain how they influence the social and political system.
C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Construct maps to represent and explain the spatial patterns of cultural and environmental characteristics.
TX 8.19(B)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Summarize rights guaranteed in the Bill of Rights
TX 8.19(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Identify examples of responsible citizenship, including obeying rules and laws, staying informed on public issues, voting, and serving on juries
FL SS.8.CG.2.5Framework: FloridaStandard: Analyze how the Bill of Rights guarantees civil rights and liberties to citizens.

National frameworks first, then state examples. For your own state's standards, ask Vera or use the prompt under Make your own questions.

    • C3 D2.Civ.4.6-8

    • TX 8.5(D)
